notice: A ceiling is the highest level this evidence could support. It is not a verified level: a SLSA Build level needs an assessment of the build platform, and an ALPS level needs an independent verifier.

levels.observed_by: The run selected the slsa attestor (`-a slsa`) and signed the collection.

levels.requires: Provenance is generated and signed by a hosted build platform and timestamped.
levels.observed_by: The signing leaf is a keyless CI workload identity (GitHub Actions, gitlab.com, Buildkite, CircleCI or a Kubernetes service account, recognized by its OIDC issuer) and its runner-environment names a provider-hosted runner, and the envelope carries an RFC 3161 timestamp. On a self-hosted runner, CircleCI or Kubernetes the level depends on whether you treat your runner operator as the build platform (formal/slsa-tracks interpretation I2), so cilock reports those as not provider-hosted.

levels.requires: Provenance is unforgeable by the tenant's build steps: it is signed under a builder identity no build step can obtain, on an isolated, ephemeral runner.
levels.observed_by: The signing leaf's Build Signer URI names the isolated provenance workflow (builder_identity on the slsa-provenance-workflow step), not the tenant workflow. GitHub Actions only: other CI signer identities are pipeline-wide.

steps.why: SLSA Build L1 needs provenance, and this run produced none.
steps.action: Add the slsa attestor to the cilock run invocation.
steps.agent_action: Add `-a slsa` to your `cilock run` command and re-run it.
steps.command: cilock run --step build -a slsa -- <your build command>

steps.why: SLSA Build L2 needs a hosted build platform. A laptop is never one. On a self-hosted runner, CircleCI or Kubernetes it depends on whether you treat your runner operator as the build platform; a provider-hosted runner (GitHub-hosted, gitlab.com SaaS, Buildkite hosted) removes that question.
steps.action: Run the build on a provider-hosted runner (GitHub-hosted, gitlab.com SaaS, or Buildkite hosted), or decide that your runner operator counts as the build platform and record why.
steps.agent_action: Move this build into a CI job on a provider-hosted runner, for example a GitHub Actions job with `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`. On a self-hosted runner, tell your human that this level depends on whether they treat the runner operator as the build platform.

steps.why: SLSA Build L2 needs provenance signed by the platform's workload identity, not a key or a person's session.
steps.action: Sign keyless with your CI's workload OIDC identity. GitHub Actions works with the platform Fulcio or public Sigstore (grant `id-token: write` and use cilock-action). gitlab.com, Buildkite hosted and CircleCI cloud work with the platform Fulcio from the CI/lock release after 4.5.0, which fetches their job token itself (on gitlab.com declare an `id_tokens` entry with audience `sigstore`); with CI/lock 4.5.0 or earlier, and on Kubernetes, sign through public Sigstore Fulcio.
steps.agent_action: Sign with the CI job's OIDC identity instead of a key. On GitHub Actions add `permissions: id-token: write` and run cilock through `aflock-ai/cilock-action`. On gitlab.com, Buildkite or CircleCI with a CI/lock newer than 4.5.0, sign keyless against the platform Fulcio (on gitlab.com add an `id_tokens` entry with audience `sigstore`); with CI/lock 4.5.0 or earlier, or on Kubernetes, sign keyless against public Sigstore Fulcio.
steps.snippet:
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: aflock-ai/cilock-action@v1.0.4   # pin to a 40-character commit SHA
    with:
      step: build
      command: "<your build command>"
      attestations: environment git github slsa

steps.why: SLSA Build L2 needs a hosted build platform. On gitlab.com that is a GitLab-hosted runner. A self-managed GitLab has no provider-hosted runner, so it depends on whether you treat your runner operator as the build platform.
steps.action: On gitlab.com, run the job on a GitLab-hosted runner. On a self-managed GitLab, decide whether your runner operator counts as the build platform and record why.
steps.agent_action: On gitlab.com, move the job to a GitLab-hosted runner (a `saas-linux-*` tag). On a self-managed GitLab, tell your human that this level depends on whether they treat the runner operator as the build platform.

steps.why: SLSA Build L2 needs provenance signed by the platform's workload identity, not a key or a person's session.
steps.action: Sign keyless with the GitLab job's own ID token: declare an `id_tokens` entry with audience `sigstore` and run cilock with no signing key. This works on gitlab.com and on a self-managed GitLab whose issuer the platform Fulcio trusts.
steps.agent_action: Add an `id_tokens` entry with audience `sigstore` to the job that runs cilock, drop any `-k` signing key, and re-run it.
steps.snippet:
build:
  id_tokens:
    SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: sigstore
  script:
    - cilock run --step build -a slsa -- <your build command>

steps.why: The envelope carries no trusted timestamp, so a short-lived keyless leaf cannot be verified later.
steps.agent_action: Add `--timestamp-servers <tsa-url>` to `cilock run`, or keep `--platform-url` set so the platform TSA is used.
steps.command: cilock run --step build -a slsa --timestamp-servers <tsa-url> -- <your build command>

steps.why: Inline provenance is signed by the same workflow identity the build steps can mint, so a build step can forge it (issue #9822). L3 needs a separate builder identity, which only GitHub Actions' reusable-workflow identity provides.
steps.action: Coming: the isolated cilock provenance workflow. When it ships, add a `provenance` job that needs the build job and signs the build's subjects under its own identity.
steps.agent_action: Coming, not yet published: the isolated provenance workflow aflock-ai/cilock-action/.github/workflows/provenance.yml. Do not add it yet; re-run cilock after it ships for the pinned snippet.
steps.snippet:
provenance:
  needs: build
  permissions:
    id-token: write
  uses: aflock-ai/cilock-action/.github/workflows/provenance.yml@{{pin}}
  with:
    subjects: ${{ needs.build.outputs.subjects }}

limits.requires: not reachable on this CI today: its signer identity is pipeline-wide, so a build step can mint it. The only paths are the GitHub Actions provenance workflow (coming) and cilockd on a runner you operate (not yet available).

levels.requires: The statement is signed and bound to the commit.
The signing leaf chains to the platform root and names a non-human agent or workload principal, and the envelope is timestamped.
levels.observed_by: Not reported by cilock yet. A leaf that names an agent or a CI workflow does not show the platform issued it (the same name appears under public Sigstore or a BYO CA), and authenticating the platform root is a separate design, so run and verify report ALPS-0 at most. A verifier policy that pins the platform root can still require it.

levels.requires: The run happened inside an enforced sandbox, and a non-agent observer signed the boundary it ran in.
levels.observed_by: Nothing yet: the alps-evidence predicate has no boundary field. See docs/design/alps-2-boundary-attestation.md.

steps.why: ALPS 1 needs a non-human principal the platform issued. This run signed with a local key or a human session, so the evidence cannot say an agent signed it.
steps.action: Enroll an agent identity for this machine and approve it in the browser.
steps.agent_action: Ask your human to run `cilock enroll agent` and approve it in their browser (you cannot complete the approval yourself), then re-run cilock so it signs as the agent.

steps.why: ALPS 1 needs a non-human principal the platform issued. In CI that is the job's workload OIDC identity, which this job did not sign with.
steps.action: Sign with the job's workload identity against the platform Fulcio. On GitHub Actions grant the job `id-token: write`. On gitlab.com, Buildkite or CircleCI use a CI/lock newer than 4.5.0, which fetches the job token itself (on gitlab.com declare an `id_tokens` entry with audience `sigstore`). Other CI has no platform-issued identity yet.
steps.agent_action: On GitHub Actions add `permissions: id-token: write` to the job that runs cilock; on gitlab.com add an `id_tokens` entry with audience `sigstore` (CI/lock newer than 4.5.0, as on Buildkite and CircleCI). Then re-run it.

steps.why: ALPS 1 needs a non-human principal the platform issued. In GitLab CI that is the job's own ID token, which this job did not sign with.
steps.action: Declare an `id_tokens` entry with audience `sigstore` and sign keyless against the platform Fulcio (no signing key). This works on gitlab.com and on a self-managed GitLab whose issuer the platform Fulcio trusts.
steps.agent_action: Add an `id_tokens` entry with audience `sigstore` to the job that runs cilock, drop any `-k` signing key, and re-run it.

steps.why: The envelope carries no trusted timestamp, so a short-lived identity cannot be verified later.
steps.agent_action: Keep `--platform-url` set so the platform TSA is used, or add `--timestamp-servers <tsa-url>` to `cilock run`.

steps.why: ALPS 2 needs an enforced sandbox and a non-agent observer that signs the boundary. cilock records no boundary today, so no run can present ALPS 2 evidence yet.
steps.action: Coming: boundary attestation in alps-evidence. Until it ships, run the agent inside the recommended sandbox so the run already has the boundary the attestation will record.
steps.agent_action: Coming, not yet available: boundary attestation. You cannot sandbox yourself; ask your human to launch you inside the recommended sandbox (https://pushgate.dev/docs/agent-sandbox) so your runs already have the boundary the attestation will record.
